questions.text: What should the architect do if an updated estimate exceeds the client budget?

options.text: Hide the estimate until bidding
Document the cost issue, review scope/design choices, update the SPPCC, and advise on cost control or value analysis
Guarantee a lower final bid without basis
Delete the specifications

questions.rationale: The source-safe response is documented cost and scope control, not concealment or a guaranteed bid.
questions.explanation: Negligent; unaddressed budget overruns lead to disputes and financial stress during construction. Unprofessional; architects should work with clients to find solutions, not blame. Reckless; unaddressed budget gaps cause construction delays and conflicts. When estimate exceeds budget, architects and QS should facilitate client discussion on options: scope reduction, quality adjustment, phase deferral, or budget increase. When estimate exceeds budget, lead a professional discussion with options—don't proceed silently or blame the client.

questions.text: When is cost specialist input source-safe to recommend?

options.text: When deeper measurement, cost checking, or value analysis is needed beyond the architect’s normal estimate control
Never, because architects cannot discuss cost
Only after final payment
Only when there are no drawings

questions.rationale: The local sources support architect cost estimates; specialist support is a prudent extension when deeper cost work is needed.
questions.explanation: Too late; construction-phase changes are most expensive. Too late; DD phase changes cost more than schematic changes. False; value engineering saves clients significant cost by optimizing design elements. Value engineering is most effective during schematic phase when design changes are least costly; post-schematic changes are expensive to implement. Engage QS early during schematic design—cost advice then influences design; cost analysis after design is fixed has limited impact.

questions.text: How should this batch treat a Bill of Quantities definition?

options.text: Make detailed QS legal claims without a source
Keep quantity discussion tied to bill of materials, drawings, details, and cost checking until a local BOQ/QS source is added
Equate it with a color board
Remove all cost questions

questions.rationale: The checked packet supports BOM and quantity checking, not a full QS/BOQ legal standard.

questions.text: How should the old schematic estimate accuracy percentage question be repaired?

options.text: Keep the unsupported ±20% answer
Rewrite it to state that exact accuracy percentages require local source support
Answer 100% exact
Replace it with a zoning question

questions.rationale: UAP Standards support degree-of-accuracy limits, not exact percentage bands in this batch.
questions.explanation: Too broad; ±50% or more applies to order-of-magnitude/conceptual (pre-schematic) per AACE Class 5. Too optimistic; ±5% requires construction documents with complete specifications. False; no estimate is 100% accurate—actual costs depend on market, labor, and contractor variables. Schematic estimates based on building massing and major systems achieve ±20% accuracy—useful for client budget approval but not for final construction cost control. Schematic estimates are ±20% accurate—use for budget approval; final estimates approach ±5% accuracy.
questions.code_citation: UAP SPP Document 201 (General Conditions); RA 9266 IRR Section 26 (Scope of Practice)

questions.text: What is the difference between a cost estimate and a construction budget?

options.text: A cost estimate is the architect’s probable cost information; the budget is the owner’s financial limit or target
They are always identical and guaranteed
The budget is a drawing scale
The estimate excludes all quantities

questions.rationale: The source-safe distinction is probable cost information versus the owner’s cost constraint.

questions.text: What does the checked packet support about the QS professional boundary?

options.text: A complete legal definition of QS scope
Only a narrow source-safe boundary: architects prepare cost estimates/BOM, and deeper QS claims need more local source support
That QS replaces all architectural documents
That QS is never used

questions.rationale: The packet supports the architect cost role but not a complete QS professional-scope rule.

questions.text: Why do cost estimates become more reliable as design develops?

options.text: Because drawings, specifications, quantities, and scope assumptions become clearer
Because market prices never change
Because estimates are legally guaranteed
Because all contingencies disappear

questions.rationale: Reliability improves with clearer scope and documents, while exact market outcomes remain uncertain.

questions.text: What assumptions should an architect state with a cost estimate?

options.text: Scope, drawings/specifications used, included systems, exclusions, market assumptions, and estimate limitations
Only the owner’s surname
No assumptions at all
Only the contractor equipment brand

questions.rationale: Cost communication should state scope, inclusions, exclusions, and limitations.

questions.text: How should the old construction-document ±5% accuracy question be repaired?

options.text: Keep the unsupported exact percentage
Ask about source-supported estimate limitations and the need for local evidence before exact percentages
Answer that estimates are always exact
Delete cost control from practice

questions.rationale: The source supports limited accuracy, not a specific ±5% range.
questions.explanation: Too broad; ±50% is conceptual-phase accuracy. Too broad; detailed specs achieve better than ±30%. False; detailed specifications enable reliable cost estimation. Construction documents with complete specifications enable accurate takeoff of all materials, labor, and equipment; accuracy approaches ±5%. After construction documents are finalized, cost estimates approach ±5% accuracy—these are used for bid preparation.

questions.text: What should a service agreement say about cost-estimation scope?

options.text: Nothing, because cost is irrelevant
What cost information the architect will prepare, what assumptions apply, and when additional cost services or specialists may be needed
That all bids are guaranteed
That PCC includes all professional fees

questions.rationale: A source-safe agreement clarifies the architect’s estimate role and limitations.
